newsitem.title: INDIA: Kashmir separatists rule out talks with new rulers.
newsitem.headline: Kashmir separatists rule out talks with new rulers.

text.p: Kashmiri separatists on Friday rejected an offer to talk with the National Conference party which swept the first local assembly elections in India's Jammu and Kashmir state since a rebellion erupted in 1990.

"We outright reject this offer," said Gulam Nabi Sumji, acting chairman of the All Parties Hurriyat (Freedom) Conference, which includes some 30 separatist groups. He was talking to reporters in the state's summer capital Srinagar.

On Wednesday, National Conference chief Farooq Abdullah told Reuters in an interview in New Delhi that he was ready to hold talks with separatist leaders, who had urged voters to boycott last month's polls.
"How can we talk to Farooq Abdullah, who is at the mercy of New Delhi?" Sumji said.
Abdullah's party won a resounding majority in the state's 87-seat assembly in the first local elections since 1987.
"Abdullah's government will be a puppet regime of the Indian government," Sumji said. "We outright reject the election results."
Abdullah has said he would like his party to join Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's United Front coalition in New Delhi.
The National Conference, which seeks more autonomy for the Himalayan state, won 57 seats in the state's 87-member state assembly. Voting took place last month, and the ballots were counted this week.

Abdullah's party inflicted a crushing defeat on the Congress party, which won seven seats, and the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which won eight. Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's United Front coalition won four.
Abdullah was expected to be sworn in as chief minister next Tuesday.
Abdullah told Reuters he would use a firm hand with separatist guerrillas, but was ready to hold talks with separatist political parties.

Indian authorities took senior Hurriyat leaders into preventive detention before the polls, fearing their vocal opposition to the elections might provoke violence. Sumji said they were still being held.
He said the Hurriyat would continue its fight for self-determination for Kashmiris. "We will continue our freedom struggle till it reaches its logical end," Sumji added.
Election officials said late results showed the National Conference won three seats in the militant stronghold of Doda, 250 kms (150 miles) south of Srinagar, boosting its total strength to 57.
Legal experts said they believed Abdullah's party, one seat short of a two-thirds majority, had the necessary numbers in the assembly to push through its autonomy plans.
